newsitem.title: UK: Europe grains mixed in slow end-of-season trade.
newsitem.headline: Europe grains mixed in slow end-of-season trade.

text.p: EU grains markets were mixed this week in quiet end-of-season trade.
The almost complete lack of interest demonstrated by the European grains trade in Thursday's European Union tender showed how the old crop year is coming to an end.
French old crop wheat prices rose, helped by short-covering and a lack of sellers, dealers said. New-crop wheat prices were unchanged as there was no signficant weather news to move prices.
Rain since the last week of April has eased concern over the impact of nearly four months of drought on crops particularly in key production basins of northern France, farmers and analysts have said.
Although dry weather returned to France this week, the crops have now enough moisture supplies to hold on for the next two to three week, they said.

Dealers played down news the European Union on Thursday cut the tax applying to daily soft wheat grain exports to five Ecus per tonne from a previous level of 15 Ecus, saying European wheat was still too expensive to compete against other supplies on world markets.
"That is just a cosmetic adjustment," one dealer said.
"The Commission just looks a little less ridiculous than with a 15 Ecus tax," another dealer said.
The 15 Ecus per tonne had been set on May 14 to discourage exports in the face of firm world prices. But since then world prices have eased.
"This reduction does not make European wheat more competitive in any way," another dealer said.
Farmers selling brought old and new crop maize prices down this week as producers started clearing up silos to make room for the new wheat crop.
Maize prices shed another five francs on Friday after the European Union granted the preferential import of 328,703 tonnes of non-EU maize into Spain.
Barley prices slightly dropped on Monday but remained unchanged throughout the week as the EU 1996/97 export campaign came to a close.

On Thursday European grain exporters placed no export bids, other than those for oats from Finland and Sweden, in the EU weekly export tender, a move that suggests the European'Union's share of a large barley sale to Saudi Arabia may be covered mostly with export licences already in the market, dealers said.

Wheat trades in Germany were sluggish as old crop sellers tried to get rid of material, with buyers, who are generally well covered, holding out for lower prices over the next two months, brokers said.
British feed wheat, which had fallen significantly over the last two weeks, was being offered aggressively.
Domestic feed wheat sellers were looking for 267.50 marks a tonne cif Oldenburg and bread wheat was offered at 282.50 free Hamburg.
The lethargy spilled over into the new crop sector where sellers saw no need to discount wheat, as their stores are empty.
Buyers were studying the progress of the new crop which looks promising, arguing there would be enough time to react to any unfavourable weather developments.
German crop weather is normal but if France underwent a drought period in the summer, this could boost German levels in sympathy.
Sellers and buyers for fourth quarter feed wheat were around five to ten marks apart with buyers at 265 marks.
Barley demand from the feeds industry was muted.
Barley sellers were still offering what brokers consider a cheap 252.50 marks a tonne cif on the new crop, with buyers at 250.

British old crop hit contract lows on the futures and was hammered on the physical market on sentiment that there is much more grain left on farms than earlier thought. "There's a lot still out there," one trader said.

But the grain is not making it to the market. "For some reason the farmers seem to think they will get a better price if they hang on, but with the harvest looming I don't see their reasoning," one country broker said.
A strong pound, and the trade's fear that the UK currency was likely to rise further, hit the new crop.
Spanish grains prices were on the upside amid short supply, although trade was quiet, dealers said.
They expected barley prices in particular to pick up as the bulk of the harvest comes onto the market, although at the moment, most available barley is from last year's crop.
The small quantity of new barley offered was quoted locally at 22,000 pesetas.
Italian soft wheat prices fell sharply over the past week as demand grew scarce and trade was thin, the Italian Institute for Agriculture Studies said.
